key_finding: REVIC didn't just take 66.76% of the votes — it deployed its own Managing Director (Kashiwagi Hisami) inside Unitika as Vice President to run structural reform, paired a career engineer CEO (Fujii) with a former Hitachi Zosen turnaround president (Furukawa) and a Kitahama insolvency partner (Horino) as outside directors. The April 2025 board reconstitution was a professional restructuring team assembly, not a governance reshuffle. April 2026 announcement: Kashiwagi pulled back to part-time as 'business recovery progressing smoothly; structural reforms largely complete' — confirms the deployment pattern was time-boxed.

directors.the_hitachi_zosen_precedent: Furukawa is on the Unitika board because he has done this once before. As Hitachi Zosen's 17th president he led the company's transformation from a struggling 130-year-old shipbuilder into an environmental-technology business he repeatedly described as 'the land-based Hitachi Zosen.' His public framing of that turnaround — 'a ¥1 trillion company by 2030' built on a 130th-anniversary 'second founding' — is the exact intellectual template REVIC is trying to apply to Unitika's 137-year history.

central_thesis_for_chapter: REVIC didn't just take control of Unitika — it assembled a professional restructuring team and embedded it inside the company for an explicit, time-boxed deployment. The April 2025 board was a PE-style operational team (career-engineer CEO + REVIC-deployed VP + Hitachi-Zosen-turnaround alumnus outside director + Kitahama insolvency partner outside director). The April 2026 announcement that Kashiwagi is being pulled back to part-time confirms the deployment was time-boxed at roughly one year. Whether the next phase succeeds depends less on continued REVIC oversight than on the three career-Unitika executives — Misu, Kobayashi, Fujimoto — proving they can run a smaller, higher-margin specialty-materials business without the restructuring scaffolding.
